rationale: Clinical cohort descriptions of RNU2-2-related DEE (DEE119) present conflicting evidence regarding pre-seizure developmental milestones and infant EEG abnormalities. On one hand, studies such as Chiu et al. (2026) and Samanta (2026) report that affected individuals display severe to profound neurodevelopmental impairment and distinct multifocal epileptiform EEG patterns, often with early developmental failure. On the other hand, Krygier et al. (2026) explicitly define DEE119 as characterized by global developmental delay with regression, and Chiu et al. (2026) report a median seizure onset age of 24 months. The presence of developmental regression indicates that some early developmental milestones may be acquired prior to loss or deterioration. Furthermore, baseline infant EEGs prior to seizure onset are not shown to be universally abnormal across all patients, meaning normal early developmental progress or normal early EEG cannot definitively exclude DEE119.

evidence.text: In a cohort of patients with RNU2-2 DEE, patients exhibited a median seizure onset age of 24 months, severe to profound impairment, status epilepticus (n = 5/5), sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges on EEG (n = 4/5), and hippocampal sclerosis on MRI (n = 3/5).

source.title: Pathogenic Variants in RNU2‐2, a Non‐coding Spliceosomal RNA, Cause a Distinctive Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy
source.quote: Patients with RNU2-2 DEE had median seizure onset age of 24 months, focal and generalized seizures, status epilepticus (n = 5), severe to profound impairment, hyperventilation (n = 3), and obstructive sleep apnea (n = 3). Electroencephalography showed sleep-activated multifocal epileptiform discharges (n = 4) and hippocampal sclerosis on magnetic resonance imaging (n = 3).

evidence.text: DEE119 is reported to be characterized by global developmental delay accompanied by regression, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and hyperkinetic movement disorders.

We show that the recessive RNU2-2 syndrome is genetically, clinically and mechanistically distinct from the dominant RNU2-2 disorder.

conflicts: Krygier et al. (2026) report that DEE119 features developmental regression, indicating that some milestones can be achieved before loss, which contradicts the hypothesis that normal pre-seizure milestones are strictly absent.

Chiu et al. (2026) demonstrate that median seizure onset occurs relatively late in infancy/early childhood (24 months), yet baseline EEGs in early infancy prior to seizure onset have not been systematically established as universally abnormal across all patients.

new_directions.question_text: What is the precise trajectory of motor and language milestone acquisition prior to the reported regression and seizure onset in dominant versus recessive RNU2-2 cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying whether regression occurs from a normal developmental baseline or on top of preexisting global developmental delay will resolve whether normal early milestones can truly rule out DEE119.

new_directions.question_text: What are the earliest detectable prospective electroencephalographic abnormalities in asymptomatic or pre-seizure infants carrying pathogenic RNU2-2 variants?
new_directions.rationale: Determining whether sleep-activated multifocal discharges precede seizure onset or are completely absent in early infancy will establish the negative predictive value of a normal baseline infant EEG.
